passages.title: Total disavowal of the disbelievers' worship
passages.tafsir:
This short sūrah is a formal, public severing of ties — not with people, but with a system of worship. Makkah's leaders had offered the Prophet ﷺ a religious merger; Allah answered by commanding him to declare, in six lines, that there is no overlap whatsoever between what he worshipped and what they worshipped, and no overlap between how he worshipped and how they worshipped. Ibn Kathir calls it simply "the Sūrah of disavowal from the deeds of the idolators," which "commands a complete disavowal of that." The six ayat hold together as one sustained refusal, sealed at the end by a line that hands each side its own path and its own outcome.

## The offer behind the revelation

The sources preserve several reports of what was put on the table — and they are careful not to arrange them into a single scene.

Ibn Ishaq reports from Ibn ʿAbbās (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) that Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah, ʿĀṣ ibn Wāʾil, Aswad ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib and Umayyah ibn Khalaf approached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and proposed a compromise: he should worship their idols for a year, and they would worship Allah for a year. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this from Qurṭubī. Ibn Kathir's commentary carries the same substance, though he introduces it as an anonymous report rather than as his own assertion: it has been said that in their ignorance they invited the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to worship their idols for a year, and they would in turn worship his Lord for a year.

There was more on the table. In a report from Ibn ʿAbbās recorded in Ṭabarānī, the pagans of Makkah offered him wealth enough to make him the richest man in Makkah, marriage to whichever woman he chose, and their own obedience to him as their leader — on one condition: that he not speak ill of their gods. And if he would not agree to that, then the year-for-year worship swap.

Another report, from Abū Ṣāliḥ on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, records a differently shaped request: "At least touch some of our gods, we will believe in you." Upon this, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, Jibrīl (ʿalayhi al-salām) descended with Sūrah al-Kāfirūn.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that these were not one conversation, and equally explicit that it will not order them for us. The pagans made these proposals "not once or in a single session, but on different occasions and in different sessions in the hope that at one time or another a compromise might be reached. Therefore, there was a need to respond to all the proposals definitely and decisively, and thus frustrate their hope once and for all." And plainly: "All these incidents might have taken place at different times and different places." So we are not looking at a negotiation with stages; we are looking at a campaign, approached from more than one angle, at more than one moment.

That is why the language of the sūrah is so absolute, and why it repeats. It was answering not a question but a campaign. And notice how little one of those proposals asks for on its face — *touch* some of our gods. Not belief, not prayer; a gesture. The revelation refuses even that. Once you understand this, the flatness and finality of the six lines stops sounding harsh and starts sounding like the only possible answer.

## Ayah 1: "Say — O you disbelievers!"

The sūrah opens with a command, *qul* — "Say." The Prophet ﷺ is not improvising a position; he is being handed one. This matters, because everything the pagans were offering was negotiable to *them*, which meant they assumed it was negotiable to him. Making the answer a divine dictation removes him as a party to the negotiation altogether.

On the address itself, Ibn Kathir gives a precise scope: "Say: O disbelievers!" **includes every disbeliever on the face of the earth, however, this statement is particularly directed towards the disbelievers of the Quraysh.** So the wording is universal in its reach but was aimed, in the moment of revelation, at the specific men making the specific offer.

## Ayat 2–5: two things severed, not one

Ayah 2 — "I do not worship what you worship." Ibn Kathir explains the object plainly: **"statues and rival gods."**

Ayah 3 — "nor do you worship what I worship." Here Ibn Kathir makes a fine point of Arabic. The word *mā* normally means "what," used for things. But the One being referred to here, he says, "is Allah Alone, Who has no partner. So the word *Mā* (what) here means *Man* (who)." The grammar accommodates the parallel structure of the verse while the meaning refers to a Person, not a thing — a distinction the reader should feel, because it is exactly the distinction between the two religions being contrasted.

Then ayat 4 and 5 come, and on their face they seem to repeat ayat 2 and 3. Ibn Kathir reads them as moving to an entirely different axis. On ayah 4 — "And I shall not worship that which you are worshipping" — he paraphrases the Prophet's ﷺ position: **"I do not worship according to your worship, which means that I do not go along with it or follow it. I only worship Allah in the manner in which He loves and is pleased with."** And on ayah 5 — "Nor will you worship whom I worship" — he says of them: **"you do not follow the commands of Allah and His Legislation in His worship. Rather, you have invented something out of the promptings of your own souls."** He supports this with Allah's words elsewhere: *"They follow but a guess and that which they themselves desire, whereas there has surely come to them the guidance from their Lord!"* (53:23).

So the disavowal is doubled deliberately. Ibn Kathir states the principle behind it: **"For certainly the worshipper must have a god whom he worships and set acts of worship that he follows to get to him."** Worship has an object and a method. Break with the object only, and you could still smuggle in the method. The sūrah breaks with both.

And this, Ibn Kathir says, is exactly why the statement of Islam is worded as it is: there is no deity worthy of being worshipped except Allah, and Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah. He explains: **"there is no (true) object of worship except Allah and there is no path to Him (i.e., way of worshipping Him) other than that which the Messenger came with."** The first half of the shahādah settles *whom*; the second settles *how*. Ayat 2–3 and ayat 4–5 map onto exactly that. The idolaters, he concludes, "worship other than Allah, with acts of worship that Allah has not allowed" — wrong on both counts.

## Why does the sūrah repeat itself?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out three explanations from the scholars, and it is worth having all three rather than settling on one.

**First — a difference of time.** Bukhārī's explanation, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports it: when two identical or near-identical expressions sit side by side, many commentators read one as present and one as future. On this reading, ayat 2 and 3 mean "I do not worship at the present time what you are worshipping, nor do you worship at the present time what I am worshipping," while ayat 4 and 5 mean "neither is there a possibility that I will ever worship what you are going to worship in the future, nor will you worship what I will persist in worshipping." Maulānā Ashraf Thānawī preferred this in *Bayān ul-Qurʼān*, and the translation rendered above ("I will never worship… nor will you ever worship") follows it.

**Second — a difference of object versus manner.** This is the reading Ibn Kathir prefers, and it turns on the particle *mā*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *mā* can serve as *mawṣūlah*, a relative pronoun meaning "that which," or as *maṣdariyyah*, which converts the verb it governs into a verbal noun — that is, into the *act* of doing it. In ayat 2–3 it is the relative pronoun: "I do not worship the deities that you worship, nor do you worship the One Whom I worship." In ayat 4–5 it is the infinitival particle: "I will never adopt your mode or manner of worship, nor will you adopt the manner in which I worship." Ayat 2–3 divide the objects of worship; ayat 4–5 divide the modes. The summary Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives is memorable: *"neither our objects of worship, nor our manner of worship, are commonly shared by us; they are different."* And so there is no real repetition at all — the wording is nearly identical but the deeper meaning is not. It adds the point that "the mode of worship was revealed to the Prophet by Allah and passed on to the Muslims through him. The pagan manner of worship is self-fabricated."

**Third — repetition for emphasis.** Other commentators keep *mā* as a relative pronoun in both places and both sentences in the present tense, holding that the repetition is a deliberate rhetorical device for emphasis. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defends this: not every repetition is empty or unpleasant. It cites *"Undoubtedly, along with hardship there is ease. Undoubtedly, along with hardship there is ease"* (94:5–6). On this view the reiteration also serves to reject outright the several proposals made on different occasions. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān attributes this line of discussion to Ibn Kathir and Ibn Jarīr.

These are three genuine readings among the scholars, and the sūrah is not diminished by any of them. What all three share is the refusal to treat a single word of the passage as filler.

## Ayah 6: "You have your way, and I have my Way"

Ibn Kathir places this line as the natural conclusion of everything before it — *this is why* the Messenger ﷺ said to them, "To you be your religion, and to me my religion." He reads it alongside two other verses: *"And if they belie you, say: 'For me are my deeds and for you are your deeds! You are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do!'"* (10:41), and *"To us our deeds, and to you your deeds"* (28:55).

On the word *dīn* here, the sources preserve a difference:

- Ibn Kathir transmits from al-Bukhārī: *"It has been said,* 'To you be your religion' *means disbelief, and* 'to me my religion' *means Islam."* Note that al-Bukhārī reports this with "it has been said," not as his own settled ruling.
- Maulānā Ashraf Thānawī, in *Bayān ul-Qurʼān*, disagrees with reading *dīn* as the two creeds and takes it instead as *jazāʾ* — retribution or requital. On that reading the ayah says: I will continue to follow my faith and you may go on following yours, and suffer its consequences.
- Ibn Kathir's own sense of *dīn*, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān summarizes it, is "the deeds of religion," which lands in the same place as *Bayān ul-Qurʼān*: **each one will be requited for his own deeds.**

However one takes the word, the ayah is not a shrug of indifference. It is a closing of the file. The offer is refused; the accounts are separated; each party will collect what it earned.

## Where compromise is allowed — and where it is not

Because ayah 6 sounds so much like a live-and-let-live formula, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān addresses a real question: is this sūrah abrogated? After all, the Qurʼān itself says *"And if they tilt towards peace, you tilt towards it"* (8:61), and the Prophet ﷺ, upon migrating to Madīnah, entered into a peace treaty with the Jews. Some commentators therefore held that Sūrah al-Kāfirūn had been abrogated, arguing that ayah 6 is apparently in conflict with the ordinances of jihād.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers on two levels. First, the argument misreads the verse: it "does not guarantee, nor does it even permit the infidels to maintain their infidelity" — it means what 28:55 means, "as you sow, so shall you reap." Second, and decisively: **"the correct position held by the majority of the scholars is that this Sūrah is not abrogated."** The compromises the pagans offered remain prohibited; the treaties permitted by 8:61, and the one the Prophet ﷺ entered into, remain permissible. It is necessary, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds, to understand the circumstances and conditions of a treaty and decide accordingly.

The line between them is drawn by a principle Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports from the Prophet ﷺ (without naming a collection): every compromise is permitted except the one which turns prohibited things into lawful and lawful things into forbidden. Apply that test and the two cases separate cleanly. The Makkan proposals, on analysis, were purported to mix elements of pagan belief and practice with Islamic belief and practice, creating confusion — and in some cases required Muslims to renounce Islam, albeit temporarily, and commit themselves to paganism. The Madīnan pact required nothing of the kind: it neither asked Muslims to renounce their religion nor to mix elements of un-Islamic belief into the true faith.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own conclusion is worth carrying: *"Islam is the religion that stands for tolerance, kindness, politeness and peace more than any other religion. However, all these ethical principles can be applied in the matters of human rights. There is no room for compromise in the matter of Divine Law or the basic tenets of Divine religion."*

That is the practical shape of this sūrah. It does not license coldness towards people. It closes one specific door: the blending of creeds, the tactical borrowing of another religion's worship, the gesture made to keep the peace that costs a piece of the tawḥīd.

## How the Prophet ﷺ used this sūrah

The sources record that he ﷺ kept these six lines close.

Ibn Kathir cites Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, from Jābir, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited this sūrah together with *Qul huwa Allāhu aḥad* (112) in the two rakʿahs of Ṭawāf; and Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim again, in a ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah, that he recited these two sūrahs in the two rakʿahs of the Morning prayer. Imām Aḥmad records from Ibn ʿUmar that the Prophet ﷺ recited these two in the two rakʿahs before the Morning prayer and the two after the Sunset prayer — on approximately ten or twenty different occasions in one narration, twenty-four or twenty-five times in another. Ibn ʿUmar also said, "I watched the Prophet ﷺ for a month and he would recite in the two rakʿahs before the Morning prayer" these two sūrahs. Ibn Kathir notes this was also recorded by At-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah and An-Nasāʾī, and that At-Tirmidhī said, "Ḥasan." Ibn Kathir also recalls that it has already been mentioned in a ḥadīth that Sūrah al-Kāfirūn is equivalent to a fourth of the Qurʼān.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds further reports with its own attributions: from Sayyidah ʿĀʾishah (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhā), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said it is better to recite two sūrahs in the sunnah prayer of Fajr, namely al-Kāfirūn and al-Ikhlāṣ (transmitted by Ibn Hishām as quoted by Maẓhar); and that when some Companions asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to teach them something to recite at the time of sleeping, he taught them Sūrah al-Kāfirūn and said that this would give them immunity from idolatry (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this from Tirmidhī and Abū Dāwūd).

There is a report about travel, too. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Jubayr ibn Muṭʿim (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asked him whether he wished to be the happiest, most prosperous and well-provided person among his comrades when he went out on a journey. He said yes. The Prophet ﷺ told him to recite the last five sūrahs of the Qurʼān, beginning with Sūrah al-Kāfirūn to the end, opening and closing each one with *Bismillāh*. Jubayr said that in those days he was the most distressed and least provisioned of his companions on a journey — and that once he acted on this teaching, he became more prosperous than the others. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites this from Maẓharī with reference to Abū Yaʿlā.)

That last cluster of details is the sūrah's own logic turned into a habit. A text revealed to refuse one merger of religions becomes a daily inoculation against every smaller version of it. Ponder where the reports place it: the two rakʿahs of Ṭawāf, before Fajr, after Maghrib, at the edge of sleep, at the setting out on a road — the seams of the day and the seams of a journey, the moments when a person is most likely to drift. At each seam, the same clarification: whom I worship, and how.

**And Allah knows best.**
